title: Reading Practice 13 - The Science of Memory
description: IELTS Academic Reading practice about how human memory works and why we forget.

stimuli.title: Passage 1: The Science of Memory
stimuli.content:
A Memory is fundamental to human identity and functioning, yet it remains one of the least understood aspects of the brain. Scientists distinguish between several types of memory, each with different characteristics and neural mechanisms. Short-term memory, also called working memory, holds a limited amount of information for brief periods, typically 15 to 30 seconds. Long-term memory, by contrast, can store vast quantities of information for years or even a lifetime.

B The process of forming new long-term memories involves a phenomenon called consolidation, during which memories are stabilised and transferred from the hippocampus, a seahorse-shaped structure deep in the brain, to the neocortex for long-term storage. Research has shown that sleep plays a crucial role in memory consolidation. During sleep, the brain replays the neural patterns associated with recent experiences, strengthening connections between neurons and integrating new memories with existing knowledge.

C Forgetting, far from being a failure of the memory system, appears to serve important functions. The brain constantly receives enormous amounts of information, and storing everything would be not only impossible but also counterproductive. Forgetting allows the brain to prioritise important information, generalise from specific experiences, and update memories as circumstances change. Some researchers argue that the ability to forget is just as important as the ability to remember.

D The study of memory has important practical applications. Understanding how memory works has helped develop more effective learning strategies, such as spaced repetition and active recall. Research on memory has also contributed to our understanding of conditions such as Alzheimer's disease, post-traumatic stress disorder, and amnesia.
